newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberia's gunmen in last-minute rush to disarm.
newsitem.headline: Liberia's gunmen in last-minute rush to disarm.

text.p: Liberia's militiamen, who have held the shattered nation hostage during seven years of civil war, joined a last-minute rush to disarm in time for Friday's deadline ahead of elections in May.
But it looked doubtful that all would hand in their weapons on time. With estimates of the number of fighters ranging up to 60,000, only about 16,000 have disarmed by Thursday.

United Nations monitors said that hundreds of fighters had clamoured to disarm in the capital Monrovia and at 13 other disarmament centres around the West African nation, founded by freed American slaves in 1847.
"Today we received the single largest turnout of any time since disarmament began," one monitor told Reuters at the Randall Street disarmament centre in downtown Monrovia on Thursday.
"We have decided to disarm and not to be caught by the deadline tomorrow," General Tedd Quiah, chief of staff of the inappropriately named Liberia Peace Council faction, said.

The head of the Nigerian-led West African peacekeeping force ECOMOG, General Victor Malu, has warned fighters that the 10,000 troops under his command would go after any of them still with arms after midnight on Friday.

"ECOMOG will be very ruthless against anyone bearing arms after the Friday deadline," he said on Wednesday. "It will be illegal for anyone to bear arms because all the factions will cease to exist as of January 31."
U.N. monitors said on Thursday that 15,519 gunmen had disarmed since the exercise began in November -- including 3,397 child soldiers and 1,028 women fighters.

Liberia's West African neighbours brokered the peace accord last August. Signed in Nigeria's capital Abuja, it followed a dozen collapsed accords and a two-month flare-up in the civil war in the capital during which hundreds of people died in an orgy of looting and fighting in April and May.
West African leaders have threatened individual sanctions against anyone derailing the deal.
Charles Taylor, the man who launched the war, and Alhadji Kromah, his sometime rival but his ally against ethnic Krahn factions in April and May, say they plan to run for president.
Their Krahn rival Roosevelt Johnson has said he plans to go into business rather than politics. All have pledged to disarm.

The war, which has killed well over 150,000 people, pitted the descendents of the slaves, grouped with indigenous allies within Taylor's National Patriotic Front of Liberia, against the Krahn who supplanted them in the 1980s.
Nigerian Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi said this week that West African peace monitors and faction leaders were trying to work out a realistic estimate of the number of fighters in the country.
"We are working on a revised number between 20,000 and 60,000 but we think the realistic figure will be between 35,000 to 40,000 fighters that we expect to be disarmed," he added.
He said that at the height of the war -- the 60,000 figure dates back to 1994 -- warlords exaggerated the strength of their forces to scare their rivals.
In the meantime, Liberia's interim head of state Ruth Perry, chairman of the state council, has been distributing cash -- $3 each -- and portable radios to disarming fighters.

"We will continue to seek the necessary international support to make sure that all of you are not left on the sidewalks. We want you to become good citizens who will run this very country tomorrow," she told them late on Thursday.
